Since this sub is so inactive, I thought I'd write my thoughts about the importance of finishing what you start.

Professional writers finish their work. This is one of the main features that distinguishes them from dabblers and hobbiests. Unless you finish, you have nothing. You may have worked on a novel for six months on a daily basis, but if it isn't finished, you can't get an agent or a publisher to read it (unless you are a celebrity, which is a different kettle of fish). Readers don't want it, either. It is literally nothing. You might as well not have started. It's like running a marathon and quitting at mile 7. Nobody wants to hear about it. Nobody cares. Nobody is going to hug you when you cry about how much effort you put into those seven miles.

Finishing breeds more finished works. Once you realize that you can finish what you begin, you will finish your work more often. It's best to start small, with a short stories or a poems. These can lead to story series and collections of poetry. When you have gained confidence that you can complete what you begin, you can move on to more ambitious works, such as novellas, plays, and novels.

All this being said, every professional writer has a stack of unfinished work. Sometimes a writer stops when he realizes he had bit off more than he can chew. Sometimes it becomes obvious in the middle of the piece that it is going nowhere, and is not worth completing. These write-offs do serve one purpose -- they are practice pieces. We learn the most from our mistakes. Nothing says "mistake" more clearly than a story or essay or novel that you decide isn't even worth finishing.

Every writer fails to finish works. Just don't make a habit of it. Remember, it's better to have 100 % of something that's second rate than 85% of something that is first rate. This may seem counter-intuitive, but it's not. An unfinished work isn't worth half what a finished work is worth, it is worth nothing. I write this as someone who has done his very best work in pieces that remain unfinished. And that's where those wonderful pieces will stay, because nobody wants to read something that is half-done. Beautiful descriptions of place. Beautiful plot twists. Beautiful character studies. Beautiful exchanges of dialogue. All worthless, because they occur in unfinished work.
